Dermatology · published research

Telangiectasia

No direct PBM treatment study for primary telangiectasia was identified. The single exact-category clinical report found improved vessel appearance after a heat-based 980-nm laser, which is a different treatment mechanism.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

No direct PBM treatment study for primary telangiectasia was identified. The single exact-category clinical report found improved vessel appearance after a heat-based 980-nm laser, which is a different treatment mechanism.

Summary of the Evidence

One exact-category human publication examined facial telangiectasia, but it used a long-pulsed, vessel-targeting 980-nm diode laser rather than low-intensity photobiomodulation. There is therefore no direct clinical PBM study of primary telangiectasia in this category. A related animal study observed eyelid telangiectasia during treatment of blepharitis, which is an indirect finding in inflamed tissue, not a trial of primary facial vessels.

Human and clinical evidence

In a single-arm study of 12 people, one to three monthly sessions with a 980-nm diode laser significantly improved the appearance of facial telangiectasias, and no complications were observed. The study had no sham or untreated comparator, and the device settings were intended for vascular heating and selective vessel treatment (Dudelzak et al. 2009).

That improvement should not be described as PBM evidence. The study used fluences from 22.2 to 146.9 J/cm² with 50–160 millisecond pulses and a small spot size. These high-energy, pulsed exposures differ from the low-intensity light protocols normally classed as PBM. Related dermatology reports sometimes record telangiectasia as a secondary feature, but they study other conditions and do not show whether PBM improves primary facial telangiectasia.

Animal evidence

No animal study of primary telangiectasia was identified in the exact category. A related 808-nm PBM rat model of eyelid inflammation reported reduced telangiectasia together with improvement in blepharitis. Because the underlying inflammation was also treated and the species and tissue setting differ, this does not establish an effect on human facial vessels.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No direct cell or ex-vivo study of telangiectasia was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The exact clinical study used 980-nm near-infrared light delivered in long pulses at high fluence, with one to three sessions spaced monthly. This is a thermal vascular laser protocol, not a nonthermal PBM parameter set. The adjacent rat experiment used 808-nm near-infrared PBM for an inflammatory eyelid condition. The two exposures cannot be compared as if they tested the same intervention.

Interpretation

The available clinical report supports improved vessel appearance after a heat-based vascular laser. It does not answer whether PBM can treat primary telangiectasia. That question remains untested in the direct human evidence identified here.

Evidence strength in source summaryNo direct evidence for PBM treatment of primary telangiectasia
Publications and records1 article

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The sole exact-category human study treated facial vessels with a high-fluence, long-pulsed 980-nm laser designed to heat and close vessels, rather than low-intensity PBM. An animal finding in inflamed eyelid tissue is indirect. A controlled study would need to test a defined PBM protocol in people with primary telangiectasia and measure vessel appearance and recurrence.
